routing.description: Route semantic and structural code queries through CodeSage. Use for definitions, references, dependencies, impact, features, context, history, risk, test selection, edit checks, and stack traces.

sections.title: Establish the project boundary
sections.body:
Use indexed retrieval when `.codesage/index.db` exists and `codesage status` succeeds in the repository under work. Otherwise use `rg`; onboard only when authorized. `help` works in any existing absolute directory. `edit_check` works in a Git repository without an index.

Pass the absolute repository root as `project` on every project-scoped MCP call. Keep repositories separate. The operator tool `daemon_stats` has daemon scope and no project argument. Reuse the global MCP registration; do not create duplicate project registrations. After upgrading, refresh the plugin and start a new host session if newly advertised tools are unavailable.

sections.title: Choose by intent and target
sections.body:
Use CodeSage for behavior discovery and code-graph questions. Use `find_symbol` for definitions and `find_references` for structural uses. Use `rg` for literal occurrences, including configuration keys, test names, error messages, documentation, and generated files. Identifier spelling does not choose the tool: every occurrence of `TIMEOUT` needs literal search; its definition needs a symbol query. Prefer the smallest query that answers the question.

Entity tools take `target`, or `targets` for file sets. `trace_call_path` takes `from` and `to`. Accepted forms depend on the tool: `sym:`, `file:`, `dir:`, `chunk:`, and `feat_` handles, indexed paths, `path:line`, qualified or bare names, `route:METHOD path`, and `cmd:name`. Use `help` to check a tool's allowed forms. Prefer returned handles and candidate choices. A handle identifies the intended entity, but name-based union tools can still return uses or similarity seeds shared by several definitions. Do not supply disagreeing legacy and current argument spellings.

sections.title: Read freshness by evidence type
sections.body:
Inspect `index.structural`, `index.dirty_paths`, and completeness before acting on structural facts. Structural MCP queries can overlay changes to already indexed files with limits of 50 files and 2 MiB of source, and a cooperative 500 ms preparation budget. A successful overlay reports `index.structural: "overlay"`; changed definitions and source are current within that measured scope. The overlay does not discover newly untracked files. A bound or failure falls back to indexed facts with `index.structural: "dirty"` and `index.overlay.reason`; `index.overlay.checked_all: false` means even the dirty-file scan is incomplete. Follow the recovery command `codesage index` when the overlay cannot cover the required scope.

An overlay does not refresh embeddings, historical observations, or feature membership. Read `index.semantic`, `index.history`, and `index.features` independently. `feature_bundle` can return current source while its selected feature membership remains indexed. Historical co-change observations survive uncommitted source edits because they describe indexed commits; new commits and renames need `codesage git-index` when current history is required. Risk combines those historical observations with structural evidence.

`session_start` and `session_end` compare current structural state, including a successful bounded overlay; inspect their freshness disclosures before trusting the comparison. `edit_check` deliberately compares against pinned Git HEAD and reports working-file divergence. An overlay never changes that contract. A bounded zero or unknown freshness is not proof of freshness.

sections.title: Interpret uncertainty
sections.body:
`counts_floor: true` means found evidence is a lower bound; zero means no modelled evidence was found, not proof of absence. Follow both the outer `completeness` and preserved `completeness.prior` limitations. `found: false` means no matching target or path was found in the reported scope; inspect candidates, freshness, and recovery before broadening the claim.

Search `confidence` measures separation in one ranked page, not correctness or a probability that code exists. The legacy coupling `confidence` and `reverse_confidence` fields mean historical conditional co-change fractions; prefer `p_cochange` and `p_reverse`. Risk scores are composite signals, not calibrated failure probabilities. An unscored field is unknown, not zero risk.

sections.title: Build the complete patch file set
sections.body:
For patch risk, test selection, and rehearsal, inspect `git status --short --untracked-files=all`, the staged diff, and the unstaged diff. Include all staged, unstaged, and relevant untracked files in the intended patch, deleted paths, and both sides of renames. Inspect unrelated work before excluding it. For a branch review, also inspect the merge-base diff. Bare `git diff --name-only` misses staged and untracked files.

Use the same explicit repository-relative path array for `assess_risk_diff`, `recommend_tests`, and `review_rehearsal`. Put the most important files first for `recommend_tests`: inputs share a bounded walk budget in request order. Read `unwalked_files`, `partial_files`, and `unmodelled`; the suggested subset never replaces required repository suites.

For CLI fallbacks, run from the target repository with individually quoted arguments. Preserve Git's NUL-delimited output if automating collection. Never turn paths into shell source, pipe newline-separated filenames, or use unquoted command substitution. Do not invoke file-set commands with an empty array. In Bash, after constructing the actual `files` array:

```bash
codesage risk-diff -- "${files[@]}"
codesage tests-for -- "${files[@]}"
codesage rehearse -- "${files[@]}"
```

sections.title: Account for cost
sections.body:
Start with one focused structural query. `help` and `edit_check` need no index or model. Indexed definitions, references, dependencies, entity cards, and exact-target bundles need no embedding inference, but graph walks, snapshots, and risk can still consume bounded work. `search` and text-target `export_context` require embeddings and may load models or run a reranker. Prefer `feature_bundle` when the mapped slice already supplies the required scope.

Read `cost.ms` and `cost.bytes` on actual responses. Ask `help` for `price_list` to see measured daemon-lifetime latency histograms and sample counts. Those measurements span projects and outcomes; they are observations, not predictions. Missing telemetry reads unknown. Response `budget_tokens` uses an approximate byte conversion, not a tokenizer measurement. Larger response budgets cannot repair a capped graph walk.

sections.title: Use recovery and operator paths
sections.body:
Ask `help` with `tool` and optionally `field` for input/output semantics, with `code` for an error, or with `intent` for an ordered investigation recipe. The intents are `review`, `fix_bug`, `rename`, `add_feature`, `before_commit`, and `debug_failure`. Use `tool: "daemon"` to discover operator tools and commands. Recipes supply explicit bindings and stopping conditions; they are plans, not automation or new authority.

When MCP is unavailable, use `codesage --help` and the relevant command's `--help` from the target repository. If daemon startup is the suspected failure, `codesage mcp --direct` exercises the single-process stdio path; do not register it as a second persistent server. Plugin review workflows remain `/codesage-review`, `/codesage-triage`, `/codesage-revalidate`, and `/codesage-report`. Read the selected command's workflow before use; a missing finding never proves a fix.

routing.reference: The [shared help catalog](references/help.json) is the authored source for this generated skill, tool descriptions, detailed tool semantics, error recovery, and recipes. MCP help embeds the same catalog and obtains field schemas from the live registrations. Edit the catalog and run `python3 plugins/codesage-tools/bin/render-guidance.py --write` from the source checkout; `--check` detects drift. Recover until the requested claim is supported, or report the specific remaining unknown.

help.description: Explain tool or field semantics, recovery, investigation recipes, and measured daemon latency. Use when arguments or evidence need interpretation; use describe for facts about code. Requires an absolute existing project directory, without an index or model. Select tool=daemon for operator tools.
help.semantics: On-demand tool and field semantics, error recovery, investigation recipes, and measured daemon latency. Select tool (optionally field), an envelope field, code, or intent; omit selectors for the catalog. tool=daemon discovers operator and hidden tools. Recipes are plans to execute with explicit bindings, not automation. Requires an absolute existing project directory; no index or model is needed.

describe.description: Inspect one indexed file, symbol, feature, or directory: facts, dependencies, tests, risk, and follow-up calls. Use project_overview for project orientation or export_context for source bundles. Ambiguous targets return candidates; unavailable sections disclose recovery.
describe.semantics: Compact indexed card for one file, symbol, feature, or directory. Includes test-aware facts, freshness, dependencies, features, bounded risk, and executable expand calls. Symbol cards include rationale, callers/callees, clones, hotness, and file import cycles; directory cards summarize a subtree. Ambiguous targets return candidates only. detail expands samples; sections selects facts. Deadline-cut sections are unscored with recover; no inference or writes. Symbol identity includes persisted callable signature fields at every detail. File public_api lists recorded public symbols and signatures, capped at 1/5/100 rows for compact/standard/full, with total, truncated, unknown_visibility, and missing_signatures disclosures; this is not a complete export inventory.

project_overview.description: Orient once at session start: languages, freshness, features, entrypoints, risk, boundaries, and test conventions. Uses structural facts and indexed history without model inference. Use describe for one entity; use search to locate behavior. Inspect freshness and overlay evidence before relying on results.
project_overview.semantics: First-call orientation with languages, file/symbol counts, freshness, a package/directory module map (files, measured lines, symbols, languages, and test share), product-first entrypoints diversified by kind, ten product symbol handles ranked by name-based fan-in, separate top_risk_files and top_risk_tests, feature summary, boundaries, and test conventions. Module line counts read current regular files within 10 MiB/file and 32 MiB/project; unmeasured_files discloses incomplete counts. include_tests merges tests into top_risk_files while retaining top_risk_tests. suggested_next_calls is removed; evidence-derived next[] routes MCP calls and recovery[] lists necessary CLI recovery. Aggregates structural facts and indexed feature/history evidence and computes risk analysis; a successful working-tree overlay recomputes rankings, while unchanged indexed queries reuse a shared ranking. No semantic search or model inference. Call this once at the start of a session to orient before reaching for `search`/`find_symbol`/`assess_risk`. Missing Git history leaves structural-only risk evidence where candidates can be scored; recovery[] requests codesage git-index. Inspect index.structural and index.overlay for the scope of current structural facts; `freshness.structural_kind` of `behind_head`/`unrelated_ancestor` describes indexed drift from HEAD. Re-run `codesage index` when current facts exceed the overlay's scope.

review_rehearsal.description: Review an explicit patch file set before committing: ranked objections about risk, tests, cycles, boundaries, and scope, with evidence and suggested checks. Use assess_risk_diff for risk alone. Inspect each objection against the actual patch; this read-only analysis does not run tests.
review_rehearsal.semantics: Predict the objections a reviewer will likely raise against a patch, BEFORE committing. Input is the patch's file list (e.g. `git diff --name-only`). Returns severity-ranked objections — missing tests, high-risk files, wide blast radius, fix-prone files, churn hotspots, import cycles touched, trust-boundary expansion (≥3 boundaries), feature-test gaps (changed a feature's core files but none of its mapped tests), and scope-spread when a patch touches many unrelated feature areas — each with concrete evidence and the files it concerns, plus paste-ready `summary_notes` (objection counts + risk summary + the exact tests to run). Pure composition of `assess_risk_diff`, `recommend_tests`, index-drift, and feature mapping — read-only, no AI prose. Use as the last step before a commit: fix or consciously accept each objection. `file_paths` must be non-empty: an empty list is rejected (the CLI's stdin/working-tree fallback does not exist over MCP).

edit_check.description: Check a complete replacement declaration against pinned Git HEAD before writing. Reports signature changes, proven incompatible callers where supported, and explicit unknowns. Requires Git, without an index. Use find_references for broader caller discovery. Does not compile, write source, or establish safety.
edit_check.semantics: Check a complete proposed replacement declaration before writing it. Parses against a pinned Git HEAD, reports signature argument counts, visibility, and same-scope overload changes, and lists only provably incompatible HEAD callers. Currently caller proof covers explicit self::/super:: paths to Rust free functions without macros, attributes, or imports; other supported source languages receive syntax diffs and explicit unknowns. Only the selected file is scanned. This is not a compilation or safety verdict. Does not write source or the index; reports working-file divergence from HEAD. Ambiguous .h dialects are refused. Persisted declaration/arity reuse requires exact HEAD content hash, language, and current structural interpretation in one read snapshot; stale or unavailable cache falls back. HEAD is still parsed for declaration selection, scopes, overloads, and callers.

find_symbol.description: Locate indexed definitions by name or target, with source locations, kinds, and author rationale. Use find_references for uses of a symbol; use search when its name is unknown. Inspect ambiguous matches before choosing a definition.
find_symbol.semantics: Find symbol definitions (functions, classes, methods, structs, traits, enums) by name. Returns exact file path, line number, and kind. **Prefer this over Grep/ripgrep for any code-identifier lookup** — one call returns the definition, while grepping for a function name often produces many false hits (call sites, comments, other namespaces) that cost extra Read calls to disambiguate. Use partial names for broad search or qualified names ('MyClass\\method' for PHP, 'MyClass.method' for Python) for exact match. For the inverse question (who calls / imports / instantiates this symbol?) use `find_references`. When present, `rationale[]` carries `WHY:` / `NOTE:` / `IMPORTANT:` / `FIXME:` / `HACK:` / `XXX:` / `TODO:` comments attached to the definition — read these before refactoring or renaming so the agent doesn't drop a constraint the author wrote down. Currently extracted for Rust and Python. Callable rows include signature with declaration, structured parameters, declared returns, and arity; unknown fields remain null and signatures remain visible at compact detail. Each overload keeps its own row. Pre-migration rows need codesage index to populate signatures.

find_references.description: Find indexed calls, imports, and other references to a symbol. Results are name-based evidence and may combine same-named definitions; missing rows do not prove absence. Use find_symbol for definitions or impact_analysis for transitive dependents.
find_references.semantics: Find all references to a symbol across the codebase. **Prefer this over Grep for 'where is X called / imported / instantiated?'** — returns structured {file, line, kind, from_symbol} rows with the reference type (call/import/import_binding/inheritance/instantiation/type_hint) already classified — `import` names the module (`./foo.js`) while `import_binding` names the symbol that import introduces (`Foo`) and, in JS/TS, each module export reached through an imported binding (`axios.CancelToken`, `typeof mod.X`, TS `ns.Type`), so a JS/TS file that imports a symbol and only uses it as `Foo.method()`, `x instanceof Foo`, or `mod.Foo` still appears — instead of raw grep hits that mix definitions, comments, and string literals together. `from_symbol` names the enclosing symbol that makes each reference (the caller), so you get caller→callee edges without re-deriving them from line numbers; it is null for references at file scope (e.g. top-level imports) or in files with no extracted symbols. For the definition itself use `find_symbol`; for transitive blast radius (callers of callers) use `impact_analysis`. Edges come from name-based extraction, so `counts_floor: true` always: an empty `results` means no reference was FOUND, not that none exists (dynamic dispatch, reflection, callbacks, and macro-generated calls leave no edge); `definition_count` / `ambiguous` / `note` say when the rows are the union across several same-named definitions.

find_similar.description: Find structurally similar functions or methods before applying a fix across copies. Matches AST shape, ignoring identifiers and literals; same-named definitions share the seed set. Use search for semantic similarity or find_symbol for exact definitions. Test files are excluded.
find_similar.semantics: Find functions/methods structurally similar to a named one (near-clone detection via MinHash over AST shape; identifiers and literals are ignored). Even an exact symbol handle seeds all fingerprints sharing its bare name; target describes input resolution, not seed uniqueness. Use before editing a function to find its copies so a fix lands everywhere, to spot divergent forks of a helper, or to locate copy-paste during review. Returns {name, file_path, line_start, line_end, kind, jaccard} ranked by similarity (1.0 = structurally identical body). Test files are excluded. Tune `min_jaccard` up for exact clones, down for looser matches. `min_jaccard` outside [0, 1] is clamped and `limit` over 100 is capped; either adjustment is reported under `_meta.clamps` as requested-vs-applied.

list_dependencies.description: List a file's immediate imports and importers. Use for direct file dependencies; use find_references for symbol uses or impact_analysis for transitive dependents. Results describe indexed relationships, not an exhaustive runtime dependency graph.
list_dependencies.semantics: List immediate import/include dependencies. imports and test_imports contain proven internal file handles; proven same-file imports are counted and omitted. externals summarizes proven Rust standard-library or manifest-declared registry/Git packages by distinct import spelling, with at most five top packages. Unknown or ambiguous imports remain in unresolved_imports with reasons and candidate handles; unsupported package resolution is not guessed. detail: full restores original product/test spellings in raw_imports. imported_by retains indexed reverse-dependency evidence. Use when the question is 'what does this file depend on?' or 'who imports this file?'. For 'what breaks if I change this?' use `impact_analysis` (walks multiple hops, ranks by distance). For per-symbol callers/callees use `find_references` (per-symbol grain, not per-file).

search.description: Locate code by behavior or intent using embeddings and optional reranking. Use find_symbol for known definitions or find_references for known uses. Path filtering has approximate recall. Ranking confidence describes score separation, not correctness or proof of absence.
search.semantics: Semantic code search (embedding-based + cross-encoder reranking). **Prefer this over Grep when you don't know the exact symbol name** — useful for queries like 'where is auth handled', 'error handling in the session pipeline', 'database connection pooling', 'where do we validate inputs'. Grep needs the literal token already; `search` lets the agent ask by intent. For exact identifier lookups with a known name, use `find_symbol` or `find_references` instead. `paths` filters are applied after bounded KNN retrieval so large MCP calls stay responsive; recall is approximate when a filter excludes many near-neighbor chunks. Each page carries `confidence` (`high` / `low`), `margin_pct`, and `cliff_at` describing the largest relative score drop in the returned rows (ranking flatness, not whether the answer exists); default standard detail omits only content below a high-confidence cliff, preserving every row and its ordering. detail: full restores source everywhere; compact omits source throughout. Flat pages retain source at standard detail. Pass `adaptive_limit: true` to truncate rows at that cliff when `confidence` is `high`; explicit response budgets may still truncate the projected payload. Pass `explain: true` for each row's score transitions and dense/BM25/reranker signals; ranking stays unchanged.

trace_call_path.description: Trace a forward call chain between two symbols through resolved indexed edges. Use impact_analysis for reverse dependents or from_trace for an observed stack trace. Missing paths do not prove absence; bounded searches may omit paths or shorter alternatives.
trace_call_path.semantics: Shortest call chain from one symbol to another: how does `from` end up calling `to`? Breadth-first over resolved callee edges; each step names the symbol, its file:line, and `call_line` in the PREVIOUS step's body. Use for `how does request input reach this exec/query/write?` or to orient in an unfamiliar callstack. Read `note` and `bounded`: `bounded: true` means a search or resolution limit omitted evidence, so a missing chain may exist and a found chain may have an omitted shorter alternative. Raising `max_depth` only helps depth limits, not resolution limits. `max_depth` over 6 is capped to 6 and reported under `_meta.clamps` as requested-vs-applied; the `codesage trace` CLI can search deeper. Direction matters: this walks callee edges forward from `from`, so swap the arguments to ask the reverse question. `counts_floor: true` always: edges are resolved name-based calls, so `found: false` means no path via those edges, never that no path exists.

from_trace.description: Map a pasted stack trace or sanitizer report to indexed source locations. Frames disclose resolved, ambiguous, or unresolved matches. Use trace_call_path to investigate graph paths between symbols; use find_references for callers. Paste the original trace without rewriting it.
from_trace.semantics: Map a pasted stack trace or sanitizer report onto indexed symbols. Paste it verbatim; Python, PHP (incl. Xdebug), Rust, Java, Go, Node/JS, and gdb/ASan/UBSan are detected per line (Kotlin parses as Java, but a frame naming a `.kt` file is always `unresolved`: Kotlin is not indexed). `frames` are innermost-first: `frames[0]` is the innermost frame of stack 0, each with the indexed `file`:`line` and the `symbol` whose definition spans it. Chained reports split into stacks (`stack`, `stacks`, `root_cause_first`): Java's deepest `Caused by:` is stack 0 with `Suppressed:` blocks last; Python's first traceback, ASan's access stack, Go's `[running]` goroutine, and each Rust panicking thread are stack 0 in printed order. Frames are marked, not guessed: `unresolved` = file outside the index or nothing matched; `ambiguous` = path suffix or qualified name matched several entries, or only a bare name matched (a lead, not a location), listed in `candidates` (max 10, or 5 for a frame with no file; `candidates_total` has the count) with `symbol` empty. `resolved` may carry `symbol: null` between definitions (`with_symbol` counts the rest). PHP `#N file(line): func()` frames give the CALL SITE of `func`, so `symbol` is `func`'s definition, not the function spanning `line`. `format: "unknown"`, `parsed: 0` means nothing was recognized. Long traces are cut twice: `limit` (default and ceiling 50) sets `frames` and the resolved/ambiguous/unresolved counts — see `note`; the response budget may cut `frames` further — see `_meta.truncated`. Only `parsed` counts the whole input. Follow up with `find_references` or `trace_call_path` on the resolved symbols.

impact_analysis.description: Find transitive callers and importers affected by changing a symbol or file. Walks reverse indexed references. Use list_dependencies for immediate file imports or find_references for individual uses. Missing dependents do not prove absence; inspect completeness before treating the result as exhaustive.
impact_analysis.semantics: Estimate which files are affected by changing a symbol or file. Walks the **reverse** reference graph up to `depth` hops (default 2) — i.e., callers/importers of the target and transitively their callers/importers — reports affected files in `results` ranked by distance and reference count. **Multi-hop blast radius from the target outward to its dependents.** `results` is `[]` for leaf files nothing imports/calls. Opt-in extras (all default off): `include_forward` adds the target's own forward dependencies in `forward_dependencies`; `include_siblings` adds same-file symbols in `sibling_symbols`; `limit` caps `results` (sets `truncated`); `summary_only` drops per-reason detail and attaches a `summary` rollup for wide blast radii. For single-hop importer/importee of one file use `list_dependencies`; for raw call sites of a specific symbol use `find_references`. `counts_floor: true` always: reverse edges come from name-based extraction, so every count is a floor and an empty `results` means no dependents were found, not that none exist.

export_context.description: Bundle source and definitions for an entity or free-form question, optionally with callers and callees. Exact entities resolve before model inference; text uses semantic search. Use describe for a compact fact card or feature_bundle for a mapped feature. Resolve ambiguity with returned handles.
export_context.semantics: Build a curated context bundle from the shared target grammar or free-form text, with symbol definitions and optional caller/callee code. Exact entities resolve before inference; ambiguous entities return E_AMBIGUOUS with candidate handles, and entity misses return E_NOT_FOUND. File and directory targets read stored chunks in path/line order; chunk targets read stored chunks overlapping their line range. Feature, route, and command targets use mapped feature files; if entry-symbol and stored-chunk lookup yield no definitions, exports collect available Entry/Owned definitions up to limit. Only a Text resolution uses semantic search. An entity without stored chunks still returns found:true and available structural definitions. A missing symbol forced through deprecated is_symbol returns found:false. Symbol entries carry rationale[] extracted from Rust and Python author comments; preserve these in synthesis.

find_coupling.description: Find files that historically change with one file, ranked by decayed co-change evidence. Use recommend_tests for patch test selection or assess_risk for a combined risk score. Missing history is unmeasured; recurring pairs offer stronger evidence than one-off changes.
find_coupling.semantics: Files that historically change together with the given file, ranked by exponentially-decayed weight (τ=180d); a pair whose shared commits span under 30 days ranks at half its weight so recurring pairs come first. Backed by git history. Use when planning a change to know which OTHER files (especially tests) tend to need updates too. Response is `{found: bool, coupled: [...], file_indexed: bool, file_commits: u32, note?: string}` — check `found` (false when the file has no git-history row), then read `coupled` for the ranked list. Each row carries `recurrence` (distinct 90-day calendar windows the pair co-changed in; informational, a boundary straddle can read 2), `span_days` (oldest to newest shared commit), `recurring` (span_days >= 30), `p_cochange` = P(row file changes | this file changes) and `p_reverse` = P(this file changes | row file changes), both lower bounds (commits touching >30 files add no pair evidence but count in the denominator); a high `p_cochange` with low `p_reverse` means this file depends on the other, not vice versa. The older spellings `confidence` / `reverse_confidence` carry the same values; they are deprecated and still emitted. Trust `recurring` rows over one-offs (one mass commit). When `coupled` is empty, `note` disambiguates: file never indexed vs. file has history but no pair above the min-count=3 threshold vs. path shape mismatch; when any row has `span_known: false` (indexed before recurrence tracking) `note` says to run `git-index --full`; when no row is recurring, `note` says whether the history is too short to show recurrence or the coupling is short-burst evidence. Index into `.coupled`, not the response directly. For the patch-level question 'which tests should I run after editing these files?' use `recommend_tests` instead (resolves test conventions + co-change in one call). For the single-file risk score that already folds in coupling pressure use `assess_risk`.

assess_risk.description: Assess one file's change risk from history and structural signals. Missing history leaves a partial score, not evidence of safety. Use assess_risk_batch for independent file scores or assess_risk_diff for patch rollups. Inspect the evidence before deciding which checks to run.
assess_risk.semantics: Risk score for changing one file: blends seven signals — churn percentile, fix ratio, blast radius (depth-2 reverse deps), historical coupling, test-gap, import-cycle membership, and trust-boundary count — into a 0..1 score. Response carries `score`, `notes[]`, the `trust_boundaries[]` list, `top_symbols[]` (up to 5 product symbols inside the file ranked by line count + resolved product-caller count + cycle membership; a row carries `shared: true` when same-named definitions in that same file share its count, `bounded: true` when resolution was capped and the count is a name-based upper bound), and `cycle_files[]` when the file sits in an import cycle. Notes are paste-ready for PR descriptions: the `crosses N trust boundaries` line fires when ≥3 boundaries cross, and the `in import cycle of N files` line names up to five members. `unscored: true` (present only when true) means this file has no git-history row, so the churn, fix-ratio, and coupling terms — 0.59 of the composite weight — were never measured: `score` then covers structural signals only and a low value is absence of evidence, not evidence of safety (brand-new file, path excluded from git indexing, `codesage git-index` never run, or history outside the indexed window). Pass `verbose: true` to also get the per-signal decomposition (`churn_score`, `churn_percentile`, `fix_ratio`, `total_commits`, `fix_count`, `dependent_files`, `coupled_files`, `test_gap`, `in_cycle`, `cycle_size`) and `top_coupled[]`; the default omits them. Use BEFORE writing a patch to calibrate caution and BEFORE submitting to flag concerns. For per-file scoring across N files in one call use `assess_risk_batch`; for patch-level aggregation (max/mean, summary_notes, cycles touching the patch) use `assess_risk_diff`.

assess_risk_diff.description: Aggregate risk across an explicit patch file set, including hotspots, test gaps, unscored files, and touched import cycles. Use assess_risk_batch for independent scores without patch rollups. Touched cycles may predate the patch; compare the base before claiming a new cycle.
assess_risk_diff.semantics: Aggregate risk for a SET of files (the file list of a patch or PR). Returns per-file entries (same shape as `assess_risk`, including its `verbose` gating) plus rollups: max_score, mean_score, max_risk_file, and lists of files in each risk category (test_gap, hotspot, fix-heavy, wide blast radius). max_score/mean_score/max_risk_file cover only the files whose git history was measured: a file with no git-history row (`unscored: true` on its entry) is listed in `unscored_files`, left out of those aggregates, and named in a summary note, so a patch cannot read as calm because its riskiest file has no indexed history. `scored_file_count` is the mean's denominator; 0 means nothing was scored and max/mean are 0.00 by convention, not measurements. Use BEFORE submitting a patch: if max_score is high or any test_gap_files or unscored_files exist, add tests, split the patch, or flag concerns. summary_notes are paste-ready for a PR description. On large patches that touch ≥5 files from one directory, per-file entries for that directory move from `files` into a `clustered_directories[]` entry (top-3 by score preserved in detail, rest by name); rollup arrays still list every clustered file by name, so cross-referencing still works. `cycles_touching_patch[]` lists import cycles (files that mutually depend via import/include/inheritance/trait_use) that include at least one patch file, each with `members`, `size`, and `max_churn_file` (best refactor target). Honest caveat: we can't distinguish cycles the patch introduced from cycles that already existed; phrase PR feedback as 'this patch touches an existing cycle' unless you've verified the base branch.

assess_risk_batch.description: Score each file in a set independently, without patch aggregation. Use assess_risk for one file or assess_risk_diff for patch rollups and touched cycles. Inspect each file's unscored marker; missing history does not imply low risk.
assess_risk_batch.semantics: Risk score for EACH of N files, returned per-file with no patch-level aggregation. Use when you have a list of files (impact analysis output, coupling neighbours, the files of a feature you're touching one-by-one) and want each individual score — cuts the per-file MCP round-trip overhead vs calling `assess_risk` N times. Each entry is a RiskAssessment with the same shape as `assess_risk`, including its `verbose` gating of the decomposition scalars and `top_coupled` and its `unscored: true` marker for files with no git-history row (unmeasured history terms, not a low-risk verdict). There is no cross-file aggregate here to distort, so read `unscored` per entry. The response also includes a top-level `_legend` short-code map: when ≥3 files in the batch share a categorical note (test-gap, no-git-history), per-file `notes[]` entries are aliased to short codes (e.g. `"T"`, `"NG"`) and the legend resolves them. For patch-level aggregation (max/mean, hotspot/test-gap rollups, cycles), use `assess_risk_diff` instead — they answer different questions.

recommend_tests.description: Recommend tests for changed files using naming conventions, co-change history, and bounded graph reachability. Put priority inputs first because they share a walk budget. Use assess_risk_diff for patch risk. These recommendations are a lower bound, not permission to skip required suites.
recommend_tests.semantics: Tests an agent should run after editing the given files. Returns `primary` (sibling tests resolved by language convention — FooTest.php, foo.test.ts, test_foo.py, foo_test.go — high confidence, always run these), `coupled` (tests that historically change with the input files via git co-change history — medium confidence, catches integration tests that don't follow naming conventions; entries carry `span_days` and `recurring`; only the top 20 co-change partners per changed file are consulted, and a note names files where more existed), and `reachable` (test files that reach one of the input files through resolved call/import edges within 2 hops; each entry carries `path`, `distance`, `edge_count`, and `via` = the changed file it reaches, in the index's spelling, which may differ from the spelling passed; sorted by distance, then edge_count desc, then path; `reachable_total` is the pre-cap count and the list is capped at 50 with `reachable_capped: true` when more exist; never repeats a `primary` or `coupled` entry). Changed files that are themselves tests are listed in `primary` and walked for tests that extend or call them (a base test class or helper under `tests/` reaches its subclasses); a `.phpt` has no grammar, so it is listed but not walked and does not cap. The walk spends one pool of resolution steps (default 1,500,000) under one wall-clock deadline (default 5 s), overridable with `CODESAGE_REACH_BUDGET` / `CODESAGE_REACH_DEADLINE_MS` in the daemon's environment. The pool is drawn in request order: each input may spend everything left except a floor (100,000 steps) reserved for every input still queued behind it, so put the files you care about first: later inputs are the ones that land in `unwalked_files` when it runs out. `reach_walk_capped: true` means the answer is incomplete — `unwalked_files` (no walk at all), `partial_files` (walk cut short), `unindexed_files` (a supported-language path the index does not hold: a new file, a path that is not repo-relative, or one excluded by `[index] exclude_patterns`), `no_symbol_files` (indexed but defines nothing) — and `reachable` is then a lower bound while `unmodelled` carries no information. `unsupported_files` (no parser for the extension: CHANGELOG.md, lockfiles, config) are skipped without capping the answer; a request of only such files returns the co-change bucket plus that note, with `indexed_test_files` and `unmodelled` at 0. When `indexed_test_files` is 0 the walk never ran and `reachable` is a lower bound; the skipped walk alone does not set `reach_walk_capped`. Two spellings of one path (`./src/x.php`, `src/x.php`) are one input, reported as first spelled. Otherwise `unmodelled` / `indexed_test_files` = the indexed test files in none of the three buckets over the total — the graph cannot vouch for them either way, so a large ratio means the buckets are a lower bound, not the full suite. Empty result means no test files in the index for these paths. Use AFTER making a change to know which subset of tests to actually run. Pair with `assess_risk_diff` on the same file list for the patch-level risk rollup (test-gap files, hotspot list, paste-ready summary notes).

session_start.description: Save current structural state before authorized edits, using a distinct session_id for concurrent sessions. Reusing an ID replaces its baseline. Inspect index.structural for overlay or dirty fallback. Pair with session_end to inspect graph changes. Use project_overview for orientation without persisting a snapshot.
session_start.semantics: Snapshot the project's current structural state at the START of an editing session. Persists the full snapshot (file count, symbol count, full file list, all import cycles, and the top-50 highest-risk files with scores) to `.codesage/sessions/<session_id>.json`, but returns only a compact summary plus `snapshot_path` over MCP so the wire response is never budget-truncated. Pair with `session_end` using the same `session_id` to detect new cycles, removed/added files, or risk regressions on hot files introduced during the session. `session_id` defaults to "default" — use a distinct id when running multiple parallel sessions. Re-running `session_start` overwrites the snapshot (useful for resetting a baseline mid-session). Structural MCP snapshots use a successful bounded overlay of changes to indexed files; inspect index.structural and index.overlay before relying on current facts. Dirty fallback requires codesage index when the requested comparison needs current structure. Embeddings, history observations, and feature membership remain indexed.

list_features.description: Discover mapped behavior slices, filtered by kind, language, or tag. Each feature groups entrypoints, owned files, context, tests, and trust boundaries. Use find_feature to locate a file's features or feature_bundle to read a selected slice.
list_features.semantics: List feature slices in the project, optionally filtered by kind, language, or tag. A feature is a behavior-keyed bundle (entrypoint + owned files + context + tests + trust boundaries) — e.g. "Laravel route POST /api/login", "Rust binary `codesage`", "php-src extension `iconv`", "CMake binary `myapp`". Use this to discover the agent-facing surface area of the project before deep-diving into a specific slice. Pair with `find_feature` (file → features) and `assess_risk` (per-file scoring inside a feature). `limit` 0 means no limit (same as the CLI); a `limit` over 500 is capped and reported under `_meta.clamps` as requested-vs-applied.

find_feature.description: Find mapped features containing a file as entrypoint, owned code, context, or test. An empty result means no mapped feature claims the file. Use list_features to discover slices or feature_bundle to read a matched feature.
find_feature.semantics: Features that include the given file in any role (entry, owned, context, or test). Use to answer "what feature owns src/auth/login.php?" — returns the matching feature records with their full file lists, tags, and trust boundaries. Empty result means no mapped feature claims this file (common: not every file belongs to a feature slice). For the curated code bundle of a matched feature (entry + owned + tests + context wrapped for LLM consumption) call `feature_bundle` with the `feature_id`.

feature_bundle.description: Read source and definitions for a mapped feature's entrypoints, owned files, tests, and context. Use list_features or find_feature to discover the feature; use export_context for other targets. Inspect found and completeness before treating an empty bundle as a missing feature.
feature_bundle.semantics: Curated code bundle for one feature_id. Same shape as `export_context` but anchored on the feature's indexed file list (entry + owned + tests + context) instead of semantic search results. A successful structural overlay supplies current source for changed indexed files while feature membership remains indexed. `primary[]` carries chunks from owned/entry files, `related[]` carries tests and context. Set `include_callers` / `include_callees` to also expand the entry symbol's callers/callees into `related[]` (reuses the symbol graph used by `export_context`). Use after `list_features` / `find_feature` to read the selected slice in one MCP call. Empty bundle with `target_description` ending `(not found)` means the feature_id doesn't exist; that case also sets top-level `found: false`, so check the flag rather than substring-matching. Empty bundle with `found: true` means the feature exists but no source or definitions were available within the request's indexed or overlay scope; inspect completeness and index disclosures.

session_end.description: Compare current structural state with a session_start baseline: cycles, risk changes, and added or removed files. Inspect index.structural for overlay or dirty fallback. Requires the matching saved session_id; the baseline remains available for repeated comparisons. Use review_rehearsal for patch objections without a baseline.
session_end.semantics: Diff the current structural state against the snapshot saved by `session_start` (matched by `session_id`, default "default"). Returns `pass: bool` (true when no new import cycles were introduced AND no top-risk file regressed by ≥ 0.10), plus `new_cycles`, `resolved_cycles`, `risk_regressions` (per-file before/after/delta), `new_files`, `removed_files`, and `summary_notes` ready to paste into a PR description. Errors when the snapshot file is missing — call `session_start` first. Snapshot file is left in place after the diff so the same id can be re-diffed. Structural MCP snapshots use a successful bounded overlay of changes to indexed files; inspect index.structural and index.overlay before relying on current facts. Dirty fallback requires codesage index when the requested comparison needs current structure. Embeddings, history observations, and feature membership remain indexed.

empty.meaning: No matching evidence was found in the indexed scope; this does not prove absence.
steps: Inspect index freshness and completeness first.
Check the target spelling and scope with find_symbol or describe; use returned candidate handles.
For literal occurrences or unsupported syntax, search the working tree with rg.
Stop when the evidence answers the question; otherwise report the unmeasured scope.

floor.meaning: Counts are lower bounds from modelled or name-based edges. Zero means none found, not none exist.
steps: Inspect completeness.recover.reason and ambiguous definitions.
Split references by from_file or resolved to handle; inspect source for dynamic or indirect calls.
Stop when the requested claim is supported, or retain the lower-bound qualification.

bounded.meaning: An analysis or walk stopped at a time, depth, or work cap.
steps: Follow completeness.recover when it gives a call or CLI command, supplying required target arguments for a command synopsis.
Narrow the target or split the file set before retrying.
Stop if the same bound recurs; inspect source and disclose the remaining scope.

truncated.meaning: Existing rows or payload content were omitted from the delivered response.
steps: Inspect total and returned in completeness.recover.
Use the supplied recovery arguments only with the same tool; page only when that tool accepts offset.
Narrow the target or request a larger supported budget. A walk cap cannot be fixed by a larger response budget.
Stop after the required evidence has been retained; do not interpret a shortened page as exhaustive.

partial.meaning: Some inputs, index coverage, or retrieval stages were unavailable.
steps: Inspect completeness.recover and per-input reason lists.
Reindex when missing or stale index coverage is the cause; investigate lexical_lookup_failed before relying on identifier search ranking.
Retry only the affected inputs and retain the missing-scope qualification until measured.

clamped.meaning: At least one requested parameter was adjusted to an allowed value.
steps: Compare requested and applied values in completeness.recover.
Split the input or use the documented broader CLI surface if the applied cap cannot answer the question.
Stop when the applied bounds are sufficient for the intended claim.

unscored.meaning: Evidence needed to compute a score or section was unavailable; absence of a score is not low risk.
steps: Inspect the section's recover and the top-level completeness.recover.
Run codesage git-index when history is missing, or follow the specific section recovery when a deadline stopped it.
Stop when measured, or label that section unscored.

stale.meaning: The response's index or referenced files may differ from the current working tree or HEAD.
steps: Inspect index.structural, files_behind, files_behind_bounded, semantic, and dirty_paths.
Read changed source before acting. Run codesage index from the project when current indexed facts are needed.
Repeat the focused query and verify freshness. A bounded zero or unknown freshness is not proof of freshness.

fields.target.ambiguous: True when the input resolved to several definitions. Union tools disclose all candidates; single-entity tools may refuse with E_AMBIGUOUS.
fields.target.candidates_total: Total candidate definitions before response presentation limits.
fields.completeness.kind: Most severe applicable limitation: truncated > bounded > partial > clamped > unscored > floor. Inspect every entry of kinds and the recovery ladder.
fields.completeness.kinds: All applicable limitation classes in severity order. The leading class alone does not replace the others.
fields.completeness.prior: Completeness evidence captured before the final response-budget pass. Inspect its kinds and recover as well as the outer budget recovery; paging and lexical index repair can remain here.
fields.completeness.recover.tool: MCP tool name for a recovery call. Invoke with the accompanying arguments after checking task authority.
fields.completeness.recover.arguments: Arguments for the recovery tool, or for the original tool when tool is omitted. Preserve explicit project and target values.
fields.completeness.recover.command: Operator CLI remedy. Run from the project; a command synopsis without required target arguments must be completed before execution.
fields.completeness.recover.cwd: Working directory for a command remedy, passed separately from shell text.
fields.completeness.recover.reason: Machine-readable cause of a limitation, including name_based_edges, unmodelled_test_edges, or lexical_lookup_failed.
fields.completeness.recover.total: Count before response truncation; not a global graph cardinality.
fields.completeness.recover.applied: Parameter values actually used after clamping.
fields.completeness.recover.detail: Suggested presentation level for expanding budget-trimmed evidence. Use the accompanying tool and arguments for a complete retry.
fields.completeness.recover.trimmed: Arrays shortened by response budgeting, with their delivered row counts and omitted row counts.
fields.completeness.recover.trimmed.field: JSON pointer to the array from which response budgeting omitted rows, such as /results or /files.
fields.completeness.recover.trimmed.returned: Number of rows delivered at this array path after response budgeting.
fields.completeness.recover.trimmed.omitted: Number of rows omitted from this array across applicable rendering passes; this is not a global graph count.
fields.completeness.recover.trimmed.omitted_han: Identifiers retained for omitted protected rows, such as files or clustered directories. Values may be handles or fallback paths/names; the list does not cover every omitted row when identifiers were unavailable.
fields.completeness.recover.shortened: JSON-pointer strings naming source-text values shortened by response budgeting. Entries are strings, not row-omission records.
fields.completeness.recover.sections: Per-section recovery evidence; each entry identifies the section and its own recover object.
fields.completeness.recover.sections.section: Name of the describe section whose evidence needs recovery.
fields.completeness.recover.sections.recover: Recovery for the named describe section; use its tool arguments or operator command according to the stated limitation.
fields.completeness.recover.unwalked_files: Inputs whose graph walk was skipped or stopped.
fields.completeness.recover.unindexed_files: Inputs absent from the structural index.
fields.completeness.recover.no_symbol_files: Inputs without indexed symbols for the requested analysis.
fields.cost.ms: Wall-clock milliseconds from request receipt through work and admission wait; not CPU time or a future-call estimate.
fields.cost.bytes: Exact byte length of the final JSON result object, including envelope metadata: structuredContent on success, the JSON metadata text block on error. Excludes duplicated MCP transport content.
fields.cost.detail: Applied presentation level: compact, standard, or full, after resolving deprecated verbosity aliases.
fields.cost.budget_tokens: Applied response budget in approximate tokens, at four serialized UTF-8 bytes per token, capped by the server's tool budget.
fields.index.recover.command: Operator CLI command to refresh a stale index. Run it in the accompanying cwd when indexing is authorized.
fields.index.recover.why: Reason to refresh indexed evidence before relying on this response.
fields.next.tool: Name of an evidence-derived MCP follow-up tool. Pass the accompanying arguments without substituting a different target.
fields.next.arguments: Arguments for the suggested MCP call; inspect why before deciding whether the call helps the current task.
fields.next.arguments.project: Absolute project path for the suggested MCP call.
fields.next.arguments.target: Retained evidence handle or target for the suggested MCP call.
fields.next.why: Rationale for the suggested call, derived from retained evidence. A suggestion does not grant authority to mutate.
fields._meta.clamps.param: Name of the numeric argument that was clamped.
fields._meta.clamps.requested: Original numeric argument value before clamping.
fields._meta.clamps.applied: Numeric argument value actually used after clamping.
fields._meta.recover: Executable retry retained by the legacy response envelope when budgeting omits or shortens evidence. It does not grant execution authority.
fields._meta.recover.tool: MCP tool name for the legacy envelope's budget-recovery retry.
fields._meta.recover.arguments: Complete arguments for the legacy envelope's budget-recovery retry.
fields._meta.trimmed: Legacy response-budget row omissions, with the same array paths and counts as completeness.recover.trimmed.
fields._meta.trimmed.field: JSON pointer to the array from which response budgeting omitted rows.
fields._meta.trimmed.returned: Number of rows delivered at this array path after response budgeting.
fields._meta.trimmed.omitted: Number of rows omitted from this array across applicable rendering passes.
fields._meta.trimmed.omitted_handles: Identifiers retained for omitted protected rows; values can be handles or fallback paths/names and need not cover every omitted row.
fields._meta.shortened: JSON-pointer strings naming source-text values shortened by response budgeting. Entries are strings, not row-omission records.
fields.error: Failure contract containing code, message, and a concrete remedy or null. Failed tools return isError=true and a JSON text block, not successful structured content.
fields.error.code: Stable E_* classification. Use help with code for semantics and recovery.
fields.error.message: Human-readable cause chain, matching the readable error text.
fields.error.remedy: A tool/arguments call, command with optional cwd, or null when the server has no concrete remedy. It does not authorize writes.
fields.error.remedy.tool: MCP tool name for the recovery call.
fields.error.remedy.arguments: Complete arguments for the recovery call, including original arguments preserved by retry remedies.
fields.error.remedy.command: Operator command to address the failure; execute only within existing task authority.
fields.error.remedy.cwd: Working directory for an operator remedy, separate from its shell command.
fields.status: Legacy failure class; error.code is the stable detailed classification.
fields.phase: Execution phase when the failure was reported.
fields.work_continuing: Whether physical work may still be running after the logical request stopped.
fields.request_id: Daemon-local request identifier, or null when no request ticket exists.
fields.persistence_committed: Whether this request already persisted a session snapshot before stopping. Check before retrying a writer.
fields.complete: False on failed or interrupted requests; do not consume their evidence as a completed result.

search.output.results.score: Final ranking score after retrieval, boosts, and any reranking or query-mention anchoring. Higher ranks first within this response; it is not a probability or a calibrated score across queries.
search.output.results.file_path: Repository-relative path of the indexed source chunk.
search.output.results.language: Detected source language for the chunk.
search.output.results.content: Indexed source text for the chunk. Response budgeting may shorten it; inspect completeness before treating it as the full source.
search.output.results.start_line: One-based inclusive first source line of the indexed chunk.
search.output.results.end_line: One-based inclusive last source line of the indexed chunk.
search.output.results.trace.stage: Name of the search-pipeline stage that produced this score transition.
search.output.results.trace.before: Score entering this stage; null when the stage introduces the candidate.
search.output.results.trace.after: Score after this stage; the final retained trace transition ends at the result's ranking score.
search.output.results.trace.reason: Explanation of the stage's score transition or skipped operation.

E_PARAM.meaning: Arguments failed validation or contradict one another.
E_PARAM.recovery: Inspect input fields with help; correct the named argument. Do not repeat an unchanged invalid call.

E_PROJECT_PATH.meaning: The project path is invalid, relative, or unavailable.
E_PROJECT_PATH.recovery: Pass an absolute existing project directory; verify access and repository boundary.

E_NOT_ONBOARDED.meaning: The requested tool requires an index that the project does not have.
E_NOT_ONBOARDED.recovery: Run codesage init and codesage index from that project when onboarding is authorized. Help and edit_check remain available without an index.

E_SCHEMA_TOO_NEW.meaning: The index was migrated by a newer CodeSage binary.
E_SCHEMA_TOO_NEW.recovery: Use a compatible newer binary; do not delete or downgrade the database to suppress the error.

E_NOT_FOUND.meaning: No indexed entity matched the requested target.
E_NOT_FOUND.recovery: Inspect returned candidates, verify spelling and scope, and use a candidate handle. Reindex when source has changed.

E_AMBIGUOUS.meaning: Several entities matched a question that requires one.
E_AMBIGUOUS.recovery: Choose a candidate handle, or a declaration line for edit_check; do not combine the candidates into one answer.

E_EMPTY_INPUT.meaning: A required file set or input sequence was empty.
E_EMPTY_INPUT.recovery: Provide the intended explicit inputs. MCP does not infer changed files from stdin or the working tree.

E_OVER_CAP.meaning: An input exceeds a fixed count or byte cap.
E_OVER_CAP.recovery: Split the input according to the stated cap or use the concrete retry remedy. Preserve all relevant inputs across calls.

E_MODEL.meaning: Model configuration, loading, or inference failed.
E_MODEL.recovery: Run codesage doctor and inspect the cause chain. Structural tools can still answer without inference.

E_DB_BUSY.meaning: The database is locked or busy.
E_DB_BUSY.recovery: Wait for the active writer, then retry the focused query. Inspect daemon_stats for concurrent work; do not remove live locks.

E_SATURATED.meaning: The daemon cannot admit more work within its bounded capacity.
E_SATURATED.recovery: Inspect daemon_stats, reduce concurrent calls, and retry after admitted work completes.

E_TIMEOUT.recovery: Inspect work_continuing and persistence_committed. Narrow the target or file set before retrying.

E_CANCELLED.meaning: The request lost its consumer or was cancelled.
E_CANCELLED.recovery: Check persistence_committed and work_continuing before repeating a writer. Retry only if the result is still needed.

E_SHUTDOWN.recovery: Reconnect after shutdown completes; check whether the interrupted request persisted before retrying.

E_INCOMPLETE.meaning: The operation could not complete the evidence required for a valid result.
E_INCOMPLETE.recovery: Inspect the cause and remedy; reduce scope or repair missing evidence. Do not treat the failure as an empty successful result.

E_INTERNAL.meaning: The failure has no more specific public classification.
E_INTERNAL.recovery: Inspect the cause chain and run codesage doctor. Preserve reproduction details; avoid unchanged retry loops.

recipe_execution.binding_rule: The server replaces $project. Other $name strings are argument templates, never literal executable values. Bind them from the named sources, preserve their stated types, then call the tool. Skip a conditional step when its condition is false. These plans do not grant write or shell authority.
recipe_execution.common_stop: Stop expanding when the requested claim is supported by current source and measured checks. If recovery repeats the same limitation, disclose the remaining unknown instead of claiming completeness.

bindings.changed_files: Non-empty array of repository-relative files in the intended patch: inspect staged, unstaged, and relevant untracked changes, deleted paths, both sides of renames, and merge-base diff for branch reviews.
bindings.target: Returned symbol or file handle implicated by the patch.

steps.why: Establish index freshness and project conventions.
steps.stop_when: Orientation is understood; recover stale facts before relying on them.

steps.why: Prioritize changed files and cycles that merit inspection.
steps.stop_when: Each high-risk or unscored changed file has an explicit disposition.

steps.when: A changed entity needs structural context.
steps.why: Inspect its dependencies, callers, and evidence.
steps.stop_when: The changed contract and relevant callers are understood.

steps.why: Check predicted objections against the actual diff and tests.
steps.stop_when: Every supported objection is resolved or reported; run applicable checks before concluding.

bindings.query: Concrete observed failure or symptom from the user's report and reproduction.
bindings.target: Handle returned by search or find_symbol for the implicated definition.
bindings.changed_files: Non-empty array of files actually changed by the fix.
bindings.session_id: Caller-chosen valid unique snapshot name, reused for session_end.

steps.why: Check evidence freshness before diagnosis.
steps.stop_when: Freshness limitations are understood or repaired.

steps.why: Locate behavior when the failing symbol is unknown.
steps.stop_when: A source-backed failing path is identified; an empty page alone does not establish absence.

steps.why: Inspect the implicated contract and caller context before forming a fix.
steps.stop_when: A reproduction demonstrates the root cause.

steps.when: Edits are authorized and a structural baseline is useful.
steps.why: Persist the pre-edit graph baseline.
steps.stop_when: The snapshot is confirmed before edits.

steps.why: Choose regression checks for the actual changed paths.
steps.stop_when: The original reproduction and relevant tests pass; recommendations alone are not verification.

steps.when: session_start succeeded and current structural evidence is available; inspect overlay or dirty fallback.
steps.why: Compare the current structural graph with the pre-edit baseline.
steps.stop_when: New cycles and risk changes are inspected, then report checks and remaining limitations.

bindings.target: Exact definition handle selected with find_symbol, including disambiguation when needed.
bindings.changed_files: Non-empty array of changed files, including old and new paths for file renames.

steps.why: Confirm indexed coverage before tracing a rename.
steps.stop_when: Freshness and language limits are known.

steps.why: Enumerate modelled uses and separate same-named definitions by resolved handles.
steps.stop_when: Relevant source callers and literal or dynamic uses have been inspected; a name-based floor is not an exhaustive rename set.

steps.why: Identify downstream files and contracts affected by the rename.
steps.stop_when: The rename boundary and public compatibility effects are understood before editing.

steps.when: The authorized rename has been applied.
steps.why: Select checks for consumers of the changed names.
steps.stop_when: Build and relevant tests pass, and literal searches account for intended old-name occurrences.

bindings.query: Feature behavior or adjacent existing capability.
bindings.feature: feat_ handle returned by list_features or find_feature for the relevant existing slice.
bindings.target: Returned file or symbol handle at the proposed integration boundary.
bindings.changed_files: Non-empty array of files changed by the implementation.

steps.why: Learn existing entrypoints and test conventions.
steps.stop_when: The implementation boundary is identified.

steps.why: Find an existing behavior slice and avoid duplicating it.
steps.stop_when: A relevant slice is selected, or none is found in the mapped coverage.

steps.when: A relevant mapped feature was found.
steps.why: Inspect entrypoints, owned code, and tests together.
steps.stop_when: The existing contract and extension points are understood.

steps.when: No suitable mapped feature was found.
steps.why: Discover an integration point from behavior and source.
steps.stop_when: The proposed integration point is supported by source evidence.

steps.why: Check affected callers before changing the integration contract.
steps.stop_when: Compatibility and scope decisions are explicit.

steps.why: Find related checks in addition to exercising the new user path.
steps.stop_when: The new capability and affected existing behavior pass their applicable checks.

bindings.changed_files: Non-empty array covering the intended staged, unstaged, and relevant untracked patch, including deletions and both sides of renames.
bindings.session_id: Existing session_start identifier, if a baseline was taken.

steps.why: Review risk, test gaps, boundaries, and scope against the intended patch.
steps.stop_when: Each evidence-backed objection is fixed or consciously reported.

steps.why: Identify focused checks alongside repository-required gates.
steps.stop_when: The relevant tests and gates have actually run and passed.

steps.when: A baseline exists and current structural evidence is available; inspect overlay or dirty fallback.
steps.why: Inspect structural regressions relative to the baseline.
steps.stop_when: New cycles and risk drift have dispositions; review the final diff before committing.

bindings.trace: Observed stack trace from a reproduced application failure.
bindings.target: Handle of a resolved failing frame.
bindings.code: E_* code from a failed CodeSage tool response.

steps.why: Choose recovery based on the actual error classification.
steps.stop_when: The cause is repaired and a focused retry succeeds, or the specific blocker is reported.

steps.when: A CodeSage request is slow, saturated, cancelled, or still running.
steps.why: Inspect active physical work and completed request histograms.
steps.stop_when: The live request's state is known; unknown telemetry is not zero latency.

steps.when: An application stack trace is available.
steps.why: Resolve stack frames to indexed source locations.
steps.stop_when: A relevant resolved frame is found, or unmodelled frames are inspected manually.

steps.when: A failing frame resolved to an indexed entity.
steps.why: Inspect the failing contract and local callers.
steps.stop_when: The reproduction and source demonstrate a cause; use fix_bug only when changes are authorized.

daemon.description: Operator discovery. daemon_stats is callable over MCP but omitted from tools/list. Hidden model helpers are CLI-internal; use public search and export_context for agent retrieval.

daemon_stats.name: daemon_stats
daemon_stats.description: Current daemon diagnostics: active requests and executions, admission/work state, bounded recent completions, caches, and per-tool non-cumulative wall-time histograms. Diagnostics-disabled snapshots still include work and project-cache state. Counts cover this daemon lifetime across projects.

recent.description: Maximum completed request and execution records, independently; zero returns counters and active work only.

enabled.description: Whether request/execution diagnostics are enabled; false means histograms are unknown, not zero.

counters.description: Started request/execution counts, outcomes, reuse, and active detail omissions.

gauges.description: Active, queued, running, shared, peak, and cache measurements.

histogram_upper_bounds_ms.description: Inclusive upper bounds for non-cumulative histogram buckets; final u64 maximum denotes unbounded.

histogram_semantics.description: Bucket interpretation: non-cumulative wall time, not CPU time.

tools.description: Per-tool request/execution totals, outcomes, and request_wall_ms, execution_wall_ms, queue_ms histogram bucket counts.

active_requests.description: Bounded live logical request records, including phase and elapsed wall time.

active_executions.description: Bounded live physical work records; one execution can serve several requests.

recent_requests.description: Most recent completed logical request records, limited by recent and retention.

recent_executions.description: Most recent completed physical work records, limited by recent and retention.

retention.description: Record and byte limits, retained bytes, and retained record counts.

overview_cache_enabled.description: Whether shared overview ranking reuse is enabled.

work.description: Current admission and physical-work scheduler snapshot, available even with diagnostics disabled.

embed_texts.description: Reuse the resident embedding model. Requires fingerprint identity and bounded inputs. Inspect help tool=embed_texts for the live input schema.

rerank_pairs.description: Reuse the resident reranker. Inspect help tool=rerank_pairs for the live input schema.

commands.why: Locate the daemon and check process status.
Read the daemon's current diagnostic snapshot.
Diagnose project, model, library, and hook setup.
Exercise single-process stdio when daemon startup is the suspected failure; do not add a second persistent registration.
